title: Wrapping & storing instruments
blurb: Wrapped and unwrapped storage limits, labelling for traceability, and when a pack must go back for reprocessing.
question: On Monday morning you find a tray of unwrapped mirrors and probes that were sterilised on Friday and kept in a covered drawer in the surgery. In the clean store, a sealed pouch is dated eleven months ago. Which can you use today, and why?

teach.body: The moment instruments leave the sterilizer, the room's air, hands and surfaces start to threaten them. What keeps them safe is a barrier between the instruments and the practice environment, kept dry and undamaged. A sealed pouch or wrap gives the strongest barrier; a covered drawer gives much less. That's why HTM 01-05 sets very different storage limits for wrapped and unwrapped instruments, and why a damaged or damp pack has lost its protection.

teach.h: How long can it be stored?
teach.caption: A 'non-clinical area' means a clinical room not in current use, or the clean area of a separate decontamination room.

teach.body: Unwrapped instruments in a clinical area last one day at most. They must be dry and protected, for example in mini-racks in cupboards or covered drawer inserts, never on open work surfaces. Take out what each patient needs before treatment starts, so drawers aren't opened mid-procedure. If you must, use clean hands and fresh gloves. Anything set out for a patient counts as contaminated afterwards, used or not. Unwrapped instruments are reprocessed at the end of the day (or start of the next), used or not.

teach.caption: Wrapping before a type N cycle doesn't work: with no vacuum, air stays in the pouch and steam can't reach the instruments.

teach.h: From clean instrument to labelled pack

steps.sub: Disposable non-linting cloth, fresh for each load

steps.sub: Links the pack to its sterilizer cycle

steps.sub: Clean area, first in, first out

teach.caption: If the pack isn't see-through, label the contents too.

teach.body: Labels do two jobs. The date drives stock rotation: commonly used packs are used first-in, first-out, so nothing goes past its limit. The batch or cycle number gives traceability. If a sterilizer cycle is later found to have failed, the practice can find every pack from that load, and, where the number is recorded against the patient, know which patients those instruments were used on. HTM 01-05 says practices must be able to show the 12-month limit isn't being exceeded.

root.label: Check the pack before use
root.sub: Every time, before it goes to the chair

children.label: Reprocess

teach.caption: Shelf life depends on the packaging staying intact and dry. Frequent handling wears packs, which shortens their safe life.

teach.body: Store sterilised packs in a dedicated clean area, in purpose-designed cupboards that are easy to clean. Keep them above floor level, away from direct sunlight and water, in a secure, dry and cool place. Never mix them with instruments waiting to be processed. To meet essential quality requirements, storage in a surgery should be as far from the chair as reasonably practicable; best practice keeps stock not in current use in the clean area of a separate decontamination room.

teach.text: 'Up to a year' applies to WRAPPED instruments only. Unwrapped instruments in the surgery last one day, even if they stayed untouched in a closed drawer. Friday's unwrapped tray is out of date by Monday.

items: Wrapped: up to 1 year. Unwrapped, clinical area: 1 day. Unwrapped, non-clinical area: 1 week.
Type B or S: wrap before sterilising. Type N: wrap aseptically straight after.
Label every pack with its date and batch or cycle number, for rotation and traceability.
Damp, torn, punctured, open, dropped on a wet floor or unreadable: reprocess.
Store clean, dry, off the floor, away from sunlight and damp, never with unprocessed instruments.

summary: You can now state the HTM 01-05 storage limits for wrapped and unwrapped instruments, explain when to wrap for each sterilizer type, label packs for stock rotation and traceability, store them correctly, and decide when a pack must be reprocessed.

A.q: Under HTM 01-05, what is the maximum storage time for unwrapped sterilised instruments kept in the clinical area?
options: 1 day
1 week
1 month
1 year
A.why: Unwrapped instruments in a clinical area can be stored for a maximum of one day, then reprocessed whether used or not.

whyNot.1: One week is the limit for unwrapped instruments in a non-clinical area.
whyNot.2: One month isn't an HTM 01-05 storage limit.
whyNot.3: Up to one year applies to wrapped instruments with intact packaging.

A.q: During unloading, one sterilisation pouch is noticeably damp. What is the best action?
options: Leave it on the bench to air-dry first
Store it at the front to use first
Reprocess the packaged item
Dry the outside with a paper towel
A.why: A damp pack has lost its barrier protection, because moisture lets microorganisms pass through. It must be reprocessed.

whyNot.0: Air-drying afterwards doesn't restore a compromised barrier.
whyNot.1: Using it first still puts a possibly contaminated item into use.
whyNot.3: Wiping the outside doesn't undo moisture wicking through the packaging.

A.q: Which information should appear on every sterilised pack?
options: The patient's name and NHS number
The date and the batch or cycle number
The dentist's name and GDC registration number
The detergent used to clean it
A.why: The date supports stock rotation and storage limits; the batch or cycle number traces the pack to its sterilizer cycle.

whyNot.0: Packs are prepared before a patient is allocated, so patient details don't go on them.
whyNot.2: Registration numbers aren't needed on instrument packs.
whyNot.3: Detergent details are not part of pack labelling.

B.q: Unwrapped instruments are kept in a clinical room that isn't currently in use. What is their maximum storage time?
options: 1 day
3 days
1 week
6 months
B.why: A clinical room not in current use counts as a non-clinical area, where unwrapped instruments can be stored for up to one week.

whyNot.0: One day applies to unwrapped instruments in a clinical area in use.
whyNot.1: Three days isn't an HTM 01-05 limit.
whyNot.3: Six months isn't an HTM 01-05 limit.

B.q: A practice uses a type N sterilizer. When should instruments that are to be stored be wrapped?
options: Before the cycle, in paper pouches
At the end of the week, all in one batch
Only when a patient needs them
Straight after the cycle, aseptically
B.why: With a type N, instruments aren't wrapped before sterilisation. They are aseptically wrapped immediately after removal from the chamber.

whyNot.0: Pre-wrapping in a non-vacuum sterilizer traps air and prevents sterilisation.
whyNot.1: Leaving them unwrapped for days exceeds the unwrapped storage limits.
whyNot.2: Waiting until needed leaves them exposed and breaks the storage rules.

B.q: A wrapped cassette is dropped onto a visibly wet floor. What should happen to it?
options: Return it for reprocessing
Wipe it and put it back in storage
Use it, as the wrap is still sealed
Let it dry and use it the next day
B.why: Contact with a wet floor can compromise the barrier and contaminate the pack, so it is reprocessed.

whyNot.1: Wiping doesn't remove contamination that may have soaked through.
whyNot.2: A sealed wrap can still be compromised by moisture and floor contamination.
whyNot.3: Drying doesn't restore sterility once the barrier is compromised.

C.q: A patient contacts the practice with a concern about instruments used at their last visit. Which record best traces those instruments?
options: The appointment book
The batch or cycle number
The waste consignment note
The staff training record
C.why: The batch or cycle number links a pack to a specific sterilizer cycle and its records, and to the patient where it was recorded.

whyNot.0: The appointment book shows when they attended, not which load was used.
whyNot.2: Consignment notes track waste, not instruments.
whyNot.3: Training records show staff competence, not instrument history.

C.q: Which storage condition is correct for sterilised pouches?
options: On the floor of a cupboard, to save space
On an open worktop near the dental chair
Under the decontamination sink
Dry, off the floor, away from sunlight
C.why: HTM 01-05 says store above floor level, away from direct sunlight and water, in a secure, dry and cool place.

whyNot.0: Packs should be stored above floor level.
whyNot.1: Open surfaces near the chair expose packs to aerosols and splashes.
whyNot.2: Under a sink is damp and at risk of splashes and leaks.

C.q: Which factor most shortens the safe storage life of a wrapped pack?
options: The colour of the pouch
Frequent handling of the pack
Storing it in a closed cupboard
Using it within the first month
C.why: Shelf life depends on the packaging staying intact and dry. Repeated handling wears and damages packaging.

whyNot.0: Pouch colour doesn't affect the barrier.
whyNot.2: A closed, clean cupboard protects packs.
whyNot.3: Using a pack early doesn't shorten its storage life.

reteach.title: Think of food in the fridge
reteach.question: Why does cling-filmed food keep longer than an uncovered plate, and what has that got to do with instrument storage?

blocks.body: Leave a plate of food uncovered and it's only good for a short time. Wrap it properly and it keeps much longer, as long as the wrap stays intact. Tear the cling film or let it get soggy and the food is exposed again. Sterilised instruments work the same way. Sealed in a pouch, they can be stored up to a year. Unwrapped in the surgery, one day. And a torn, damp or dropped pouch has lost its 'cling film', so it goes back to be reprocessed.

blocks.text: Unwrapped instruments that were set out for a patient count as contaminated afterwards, even if nobody touched them.

explain.body: Wrapped: up to 1 year. Unwrapped in the clinical area: 1 day. Unwrapped in a non-clinical area (a clinical room not in use, or the clean area of a decontamination room): 1 week.

test.q: What is the maximum storage time for wrapped instruments whose packaging remains intact?
options: 1 week
1 month
6 months
Up to 1 year
test.why: HTM 01-05 says wrapped instruments may be stored for up to one year, provided the packaging stays intact.

whyNot.0: One week is the unwrapped, non-clinical limit.
whyNot.1: One month isn't an HTM 01-05 limit.
whyNot.2: Six months isn't an HTM 01-05 storage limit.

explain.body: Dry, protected (covered drawer inserts or mini-racks in cupboards), never on open surfaces. Reprocessed at the end of the day, or the start of the next, whether used or not.

rows.label: Tray left on the open worktop
Kept unused for three days in the surgery

test.q: Unwrapped instruments in the surgery weren't used today. What should happen to them at the end of the day?
options: Keep them for tomorrow's first patient
Reprocess them, used or not
Move them to an open shelf
Wrap them and store for a year
test.why: Unwrapped instruments in the clinical area are reprocessed at the end of the working day (or start of the next), regardless of whether they were used.

whyNot.0: That would exceed the one-day limit.
whyNot.2: Open surfaces are never acceptable for unwrapped instruments.
whyNot.3: They must be reprocessed, not just wrapped as they are.

explain.body: Date for storage limits and first-in, first-out rotation. Batch or cycle number to trace the pack to its sterilizer cycle, and to the patient where recorded.

test.q: What is the main reason for dating sterilised packs?
options: To support stock rotation and limits
To show who sealed the pack
To record the patient's visit date
To meet the waste regulations
test.why: Dating lets the practice use older packs first and ensure none exceed their storage limit.

whyNot.1: Operator details go in the logbook, not usually on the pack.
whyNot.2: Packs are dated when processed, not by patient visit.
whyNot.3: Waste regulations don't govern instrument pack labels.

explain.body: Before any pack goes to the chair: packaging intact and dry, seal closed, label readable, in date, indicator changed. Any failure means reprocess.

test.q: A sealed pouch in the drawer has a small puncture. What is the best action?
options: Cover the hole with autoclave tape
Use it if the instrument looks clean
Reprocess the instrument
Use it on the next patient only
test.why: A puncture breaks the barrier, so the contents can no longer be considered sterile; the instrument is reprocessed.

whyNot.0: Tape doesn't restore a sterile barrier.
whyNot.3: No patient should receive instruments from a compromised pack.
